Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I Immense, august, like some Titanic bloom, The mighty choir unfolds its lithic core, Petalled with panes of azure, gules and or, Splendidly lambent in the Gothic gloom, And stamened with keen flamelets that illume The pale high-altar. On the prayer-worn floor, By worshippers innumerous thronged of yore, A few brown crones, familiars of the tomb, The stranded driftwood of Faith’s ebbing sea— For these alone the finials fret the skies, The topmost bosses shake their blossoms free, While from the triple portals, with grave eyes, Tranquil, and fixed upon eternity, The cloud of witnesses still testifies. II The crimson panes like blood-drops stigmatise The western floor. The aisles are mute and cold. A rigid fetich in her robe of gold, The Virgin of the Pillar, with blank eyes, Enthroned beneath her votive canopies, Gathers a meagre remnant to her fold. The rest is solitude; the church, grown old, Stands stark and grey beneath the burning skies. Well-nigh again its mighty framework grows To be a part of nature’s self, withdrawn From hot humanity’s impatient woes; The floor is ridged like some rude mountain lawn, And in the east one giant window shows The roseate coldness of an Alp at dawn.

Here are two ways to present your polished text, depending on your needs: 

**Option 1** restores the text to its proper poetic structure (two sonnets in iambic pentameter) with refined lineation and typography. 

**Option 2** adapts the poetic imagery into a seamless, highly eloquent prose piece suitable for a essay, program guide, or literary description.

---

### Option 1: Formatted Poetic Verse (Recommended)

**I**

Immense, august, like some Titanic bloom,  
The mighty choir unfolds its lithic core,  
Petalled with panes of azure, gules, and or,  
Splendidly lambent in the Gothic gloom,  
And stamened with keen flamelets that illume  
The pale high-altar. On the prayer-worn floor,  
By worshippers innumerous thronged of yore,  
A few brown crones—familiars of the tomb,  
The stranded driftwood of Faith’s ebbing sea—  
For these alone the finials fret the skies,  
The topmost bosses shake their blossoms free;  
While from the triple portals, with grave eyes,  
Tranquil, and fixed upon eternity,  
The cloud of witnesses still testifies.  

**II**

The crimson panes like blood-drops stigmatise  
The western floor. The aisles are mute and cold.  
A rigid fetish in her robe of gold,  
The Virgin of the Pillar, with blank eyes,  
Enthroned beneath her votive canopies,  
Gathers a meagre remnant to her fold.  
The rest is solitude; the church, grown old,  
Stands stark and grey beneath the burning skies.  

Well-nigh again its mighty framework grows  
To be a part of nature’s self, withdrawn  
From hot humanity’s impatient woes;  
The floor is ridged like some rude mountain lawn,  
And in the east one giant window shows  
The roseate coldness of an Alp at dawn.

---

### Option 2: Eloquent Prose Adaptation

> **Part I**  
> Immense and august, like some colossal bloom, the mighty choir unfolds its stone core. It is petaled with stained glass of azure, crimson, and gold—splendidly radiant amidst the Gothic gloom—and stamened with sharp, flickering flames that illuminate the pale high altar. Upon the prayer-worn floor, once thronged by countless worshippers in ages past, sit only a few elderly women: quiet regulars of the shadows and the stranded driftwood of faith’s receding tide. For them alone do the soaring finials carve the sky and the highest carved bosses unfurl their stone blossoms. Meanwhile, from the triple portals, a silent cloud of witnesses looks on with grave, tranquil eyes, their gazes fixed unwaveringly upon eternity.
> 
> **Part II**  
> Sunlight through the crimson panes casts blood-like stains across the western floor, while the surrounding aisles remain silent and cold. Enthroned beneath her votive canopy, a rigid, gold-robed figure of the Virgin of the Pillar gazes out with blank eyes, gathering only a meager remnant of the faithful to her fold. All else is solitude. The ancient cathedral stands stark and gray beneath the scorching sky, its massive framework gradually reclaiming its place within nature—withdrawn at last from the restless anxieties of modern humanity. The stone floor has grown uneven, ridged like a rugged mountain meadow, while in the east, a single monumental window reveals the pale, rosy chill of an Alpine sunrise.

**The Sanctuary of Stone and Shadow**

Beneath a bruised twilight sky, the ancient cathedral stands as a monument forged in stone and memory. Its soaring Gothic arches and skeletal flying buttresses cut a dramatic silhouette against the horizon, evoking an era when every chisel mark was driven by a fervent desire to bridge the gap between heaven and earth. Step across its worn threshold, however, and the grand narrative of its past immediately collides with the profound stillness of its present. Where centuries of liturgical chants once thundered off vaulted ceilings, a heavy, reverent silence now settles over the nave, carrying only the faint, ghostly whispers of a bygone spiritual epoch.

The interior of the sanctuary offers a striking study in contrasts. Sunlight filters through magnificent rose windows, casting fractured beams of cobalt, crimson, and gold across dust-moted air. These rich colors illuminate relics of former magnificence: peeling gold leaf on the high altar, intricately carved oak pews that stretch into darkness, and the silent, towering pipes of an organ that once shook the very foundations of the valley. Yet, the vastness of the space only emphasizes its emptiness. The vibrant congregation that once packed these aisles—seeking solace, offering penance, and celebrating communal sacred rites—has dissolved with the passage of time. The cathedral’s history of grand devotion is now framed by stark solitude, a physical testament to the quiet recession of religious faith from the center of human life.

In this expansive void, the human presence has dwindled to a fragile remnant. A small handful of worshippers, their heads bowed and coats pulled tight against the draft, sit scattered among the rows of empty pews. Their soft, rustling prayers are faint ripples in an ocean of silence, barely echoing off the towering walls. This modest gathering reflects the fading twilight of institutional worship: a quiet, persistent fidelity enduring within a space designed for thousands. The contrast between the cathedral’s immense physical capacity and its few remaining devotees poignantly underscores the transience of human institutions and the shifting tides of cultural devotion.

Yet, as human attendance fades, the structure itself embarks on a profound transformation. Far from being merely a decaying vessel of lost faith, the aging cathedral reveals a deeper, more resilient identity. As human maintenance retreats, the boundaries between the artificial monument and the living environment begin to blur. Weathered limestone walls, carved by medieval masons, are slowly reclaimed by the elements. Green tendrils of ivy scale the vertical heights of the spires, weaving through stone tracery, while thick carpets of velvety moss anchor themselves in the crevices of the outer walls.

Birds now make their homes within the hollowed gaze of stone saints, their calls filling the high vaults where choirs once sang. Rain and wind gently smooth the sharp contours of gargoyles and angels, gradually dissolving the distinctions between sacred architecture and raw geological form. In this slow, graceful integration, the cathedral transcends the fleeting nature of human purpose. While the devotion that built it may wane, the majestic stone sanctuary does not fall into meaningless ruin; instead, it is steadily reabsorbed, finding a quiet, permanent communion within the timeless and enduring realm of the natural world.

counterfactuals.output:
**I. The Gloaming of the Sanctuary**

High in the vaulted gloom, dark shadows creep
Through shattered panes where wounded rubies shine;
The pale, forgotten martyrs of the line
In faint, slow languor softly drift to sleep.
No swing of censer wakes the silent deep,
No vesper hymn exalts the cold design;
The god hath spilled his sacrament of wine,
And left his desolate elect to weep.

Yet Art abides within this strange decay,
A jeweled corpse upon a throne of stone,
Where fading sunlight bleeds its last desire;
Faith dies in silence as the shadows sway,
And amethyst and lazuli, alone,
In dim, decadent agonies expire.


**II. The Verdant Sepulchre**

Outside, the ivy weaves a pall of green
Across the carven gargoyle’s leering stone;
Wild lichen crowns the high, deserted throne
Where once the blessed Virgin stood as queen.
The towering vaults, once solemn and serene,
Now mirror leafy bowers, overgrown;
Great roots unbind the pavement, bone by bone,
To claim the sanctuary, dark, unseen.

A choir of birds supplants the chant of old,
The altar turns to fern and forest floor,
As nature drapes her emerald counterpane.
Man’s proud devotion stiffens in the cold,
While ruin weaves a temple evermore,
And Pan awakes where Christ no more shall reign.

counterfactuals.prompt: Two sonnets about a gothic cathedral fading into history.
counterfactuals.output:
**I. The Ruin on the Ridge**

High spires that pierced the pale, forgiving sky,
Now fracture under Time’s unyielding hand;
Upon the ridge the hollow shadows stand,
Where silent gargoyles watch the ages die.
No longer do the choral anthems cry,
Nor sweet-breathed incense drift across the land;
The sacred ash is scattered in the sand,
And broken saints in lonely ruin lie.

The stained-glass sun that burned in holy red
Now yields its light to ivy's quiet reign;
The vaulted nave yields up its fallen cross.
Forgotten are the tears the mourners bled,
Forgotten is the song of joy and pain,
As history reclaims the sacred loss.


**II. The Skeletal Temple**

The buttresses, like ribs of some great beast,
Collapse beneath the weight of quiet years;
The altar faces toward a phantom east,
Where none remain to weep their final tears.

The names of masons carved upon the grain
Are washed away by centuries of storm;
What once was built to outlast human pain
Dissolves back into dark, forgotten form.

Night wraps the nave in shrouds of silver mist,
As wild vines reclaim the flagstone floor;
The soaring heights that sun and starlight kissed
Are whispers now, remembered nevermore.

Thus grandest shrines, though raised to touch the sky,
Must bend to time, and fade, and softly die.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

**I. The Shell of Stone**

High o’er the sleepy roofs the finials spire,
Chiseled in lace by some forgotten hand,
Where once the nave, a towering, holy strand,
Echoed the anthems of a white-robed choir.
Deep in the vaulting, bound in leafy wire,
The stony bosses of that shadowed land
Turn black with dust; the figures grim and grand
Fade in the twilight of a dying fire.

The flying buttresses, like ribs of stone,
Uphold the clerestory’s hollow, ruined grace,
While gargoyles sneer into the lifeless sky;
The pride of medieval faith, overthrown,
Has left upon the altar’s silent face
This lapidary relic, doomed to die.


**II. The Vanished Light**

Yet through the rose-window the sunset pours
Cold light of cobalt, amethyst, and gules,
Mocking the twilight of forgotten schools,
To stain with blood the silent marble floors.
Rain rushes through the high, uncurtained doors,
Where sacred chalices and silver tools
Lie lost; no longer any bishop rules
These desolate and unremembered shores.

No longer does the golden censer swing
To cloud the rood-screen with a scented breath,
Nor kneeling crowds adore the Host divine;
Only the sun, an unrepenting king,
Casts jeweled shadows in the vault of death,
And gilds the corpse of a forgotten shrine.
